specPoints.text: understand, in terms of changes in oxidation number, the following reactions of the halogens: i oxidation reactions with Group 1 and 2 metals ii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with water and the use of chlorine in water treatment iii the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to form bleach iv the disproportionation reaction of chlorine with hot alkali v reactions analogous to those specified above

primer.text: Halogens duel for electrons, and the stronger fighter always wins. This note sets out the displacement rule, works the ionic equations that expose the electron transfer, and reads the colour evidence - aqueous shades and organic-layer purples - that turns test-tube observations into halide identification.

lessons.title: The displacement ladder of the halogens
lessons.opening: Drop chlorine water into bromide solution and the chlorine robs bromide of its place. Displacement reactions are the reactivity ladder made visible: a halogen higher in Group 7 pushes a lower one out of its salt, and every such contest is a redox reaction.
keyPoints: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its halide.
Chlorine displaces bromine from bromide solution and iodine from iodide solution.
Bromine displaces iodine from iodide solution, but cannot touch chloride.
Each displacement is a redox reaction: the displaced halogen is oxidised while the displacing halogen is reduced.
Spectator ions such as sodium or potassium are removed to write the ionic equation.

low.restatement: The higher halogen wins the electron tug-of-war: chlorine takes bromide's electron, bromine takes iodide's, but nothing lower can take from anything higher.
low.analogy: Like a stronger magnet pulling pins off a weaker magnet - the pins (electrons) always move towards the stronger pull, never backwards.
low.examPointer: Write the ionic equation with the spectator ions removed, e.g. Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2, and label the oxidation-number changes for full marks.

medium.restatement: The displacing halogen drops from oxidation number 0 to -1 (reduction) while the displaced halide climbs from -1 to 0 (oxidation), so electron transfer is explicit in the ionic equation.
medium.analogy: Two climbers swap positions on a ladder: one descends two rungs (gains electrons), the other climbs two rungs (loses them), and the ladder's total is unchanged.
medium.examPointer: Quote the electron ledger, not just colour change, when the question says 'show that this is a redox reaction'.

check.stem: Which halogen can displace iodine from potassium iodide solution?

options.text: Chlorine, because it sits above iodine and is more reactive
options.explanation: The higher, more reactive halogen displaces the lower one from its halide solution.

options.text: Bromine only, because iodine cannot be displaced
options.explanation: Bromine also displaces iodine; any halogen above iodine succeeds.

options.text: Iodine, because like displaces like
options.explanation: A halogen cannot displace its own kind - no electron transfer occurs.

options.text: Fluorine cannot, because it is too reactive
options.explanation: Fluorine sits above iodine and would displace it; reactivity helps, not blocks.

check.stem: In Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2 the bromide ions are

options.text: Oxidised, rising from oxidation number -1 to 0
options.explanation: Each bromide loses an electron to chlorine, the defining change of oxidation.

options.text: Reduced, falling from 0 to -1
options.explanation: That is the chlorine change, not the bromide change.

options.text: Spectators, because their oxidation number never changes
options.explanation: Bromide's oxidation number changes from -1 to 0, so it reacts.

options.text: Precipitated out of solution as a solid
options.explanation: Bromine stays dissolved; no precipitate forms here.

check.stem: Why are sodium ions absent from the ionic equation?

options.text: They are spectator ions whose oxidation numbers stay +1 throughout
options.explanation: Unchanged species are stripped from the ionic equation to show the actual electron transfer.

options.text: They evaporate with the chlorine water
options.explanation: Sodium ions remain dissolved; they are simply not part of the redox change.

options.text: They react to form sodium gas
options.explanation: No such product exists in these displacement reactions.

options.text: They are too large to take part in solution reactions
options.explanation: Size is irrelevant; the reason is their unchanged oxidation state.

check.stem: Adding bromine water to potassium chloride solution will produce

options.text: No displacement, because bromine is below chlorine in the group
options.explanation: The lower halogen cannot oxidise the chloride ion of a higher halogen.

options.text: Chlorine gas, because bromine displaces chlorine
options.explanation: Displacement only runs downhill the reactivity ladder.

options.text: Bromide ions, because chloride donates electrons
options.explanation: Chloride would have to be oxidised, which bromine cannot achieve.

options.text: A brown solution of iodine
options.explanation: Iodine is not involved in this mixture at all.

check.stem: Which ionic equation represents bromine displacing iodine?

options.explanation: Bromine molecules take one electron from each iodide, giving bromide ions and iodine molecules.

options.text: Br2 + I- -> Br- + I2
options.explanation: The equation is not balanced in charge or atoms: two iodides are needed per bromine molecule.
That is iodine displacing bromide, the reverse of the asked reaction.

options.text: Br2 + 2KI -> 2KBr + I2
options.explanation: That is the full equation; the ionic form removes the potassium spectators.

check.stem: State the rule linking halogen reactivity to displacement.
check.modelAnswer: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of that halogen's halide ions.

check.stem: Write the ionic equation for chlorine displacing bromine from bromide ions.
check.modelAnswer: Cl2 (aq) + 2Br- (aq) -> 2Cl- (aq) + Br2 (aq), with sodium or potassium spectators removed.

check.stem: Explain why displacement reactions of the halogens are redox reactions.
check.modelAnswer: The displacing halogen's oxidation number falls from 0 to -1 as it gains electrons, while the displaced halide's rises from -1 to 0 as it loses them, so both reduction and oxidation occur together.

check.stem: A mixture gives a brown colour when chlorine water is added, then turns purple in an organic layer. Identify the halide present and justify your answer.
check.modelAnswer: Iodide is present: chlorine oxidises iodide to iodine, which colours the aqueous layer brown and concentrates as a purple solution in the added organic solvent, matching the known iodine observations.

lessons.title: Observing displacements: aqueous colours and the organic layer
lessons.opening: Displacement announces itself in colour: yellow-orange for bromine, brown for iodine in water, and a dramatic purple iodine shade once an organic solvent collects the halogen. This lesson converts those observations into positive halide identification.
keyPoints: Chlorine solution added to potassium bromide gives a yellow-orange colour as bromine forms.
Chlorine solution added to potassium iodide gives a brown colour in water, and iodine appears purple in an organic solvent layer.
An organic solvent such as cyclohexane concentrates the halogen products, making the colour changes easier to see.
Bromine displacing iodine likewise gives brown in water and purple in the organic layer.

low.restatement: Each successful displacement paints its product colour: bromine yellow-orange, iodine brown in water but purple when shaken into an organic layer, where halogens dissolve more readily.
low.analogy: The organic solvent is a spotlight that gathers the scattered halogen into one vivid  puddle of colour for the eye to judge.
low.examPointer: Quote both the aqueous colour and the organic-layer colour when identifying the halide - examiners award the mark for the paired observations.

medium.restatement: The halogen products differ in solubility preference: they favour the organic phase, so adding cyclohexane extracts the halogen and sharpens the diagnostic colour. The colour itself tracks the identity of the displaced halogen, not the reagent.
medium.analogy: Like separating oil droplets from water: the halogen gathers into its preferred layer and the colour intensifies enough to read unambiguously.
medium.examPointer: Do not confuse bromine's aqueous brown with iodine's purple organic layer - mislabelled colours lose the identification mark.

check.stem: What colour appears when chlorine solution reacts with potassium bromide solution?

options.text: Yellow-orange, as bromine is formed
options.explanation: The liberated bromine colours the mixture yellow-orange.

options.text: Purple, as iodine is formed
options.explanation: Iodine is not a product here; bromine is.

options.text: White precipitate, as bromide precipitates
options.explanation: No precipitate forms; the halogens stay dissolved.

options.text: Pale green, as chlorine accumulates
options.explanation: The chlorine is consumed into chloride ions, not accumulated.

check.stem: Adding an organic solvent such as cyclohexane helps because

options.text: Halogens are more soluble in the organic layer, concentrating the colour there
options.explanation: The halogen product partitions into the organic phase, sharpening the observation.

options.text: It converts the halogen into a more reactive form
options.explanation: The solvent does not change the chemistry, only where the product collects.

options.text: It neutralises the leftover halide ions
options.explanation: Cyclohexane is not a reagent for the ions; it is an extraction aid.

options.text: It prevents the halogen from evaporating
options.explanation: Volatility is unaffected; visibility is the gain.

check.stem: Bromine added to potassium iodide solution gives which pair of observations?

options.text: Brown solution in water, purple organic layer with cyclohexane
options.explanation: Iodine forms brown in water and partitions purple into the organic solvent.

options.text: Yellow-orange solution, colourless organic layer
options.explanation: Those are bromine's colours, not iodine's.

options.text: White precipitate, then dissolving in ammonia
options.explanation: Precipitates belong to silver halide tests, not displacement colours.

options.text: No visible change, because bromine cannot displace iodine
options.explanation: Bromine sits above iodine and does displace it.

check.stem: In the bromine-iodide displacement, the electron ledger shows

options.text: Each iodide loses one electron while each bromine atom gains one, two electrons in total moving
options.explanation: 2I- -> I2 loses two electrons; Br2 + 2e- -> 2Br- gains the same two.

options.text: Four electrons moving, two per iodide ion
options.explanation: Each iodide loses exactly one electron to reach iodine's oxidation number 0.

options.text: No electron transfer, as this is not a redox process
options.explanation: The oxidation numbers of both halogens change, so transfer occurs.

options.text: Electrons moving from bromine to iodide
options.explanation: The flow runs from iodide to bromine, downhill the reactivity ladder.

check.stem: Which halide ion could NOT be identified by a colour change on adding chlorine water?

options.text: Chloride, because chlorine cannot displace its own kind from solution
options.explanation: Chlorine is already the displacing reagent; chloride gives no colour change with it.

options.text: Bromide, which turns yellow-orange
options.explanation: Bromide does give a colour change and so is identifiable.

options.text: Iodide, which turns brown then purple
options.explanation: Iodide is identifiable by the iodine colours.

options.text: Fluoride, which would be oxidised to pale fluorine
options.explanation: Fluorine is above chlorine; it cannot be displaced by it at all.

check.stem: State the colour of iodine in an organic solvent layer after displacement.
check.modelAnswer: Purple, once the iodine partitions into the added organic solvent such as cyclohexane.

check.stem: State the colour changes when bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution.
check.modelAnswer: The aqueous mixture turns brown as iodine forms, and the layer becomes purple if an organic solvent is added.

check.stem: Explain why the same halogen can show different colours in water and in an organic solvent.
check.modelAnswer: The halogen product partitions preferentially into the organic layer, where it is more soluble and more concentrated, and its visible colour there differs from the dilute aqueous shade.

check.stem: Two unknown halide solutions both turn brown with chlorine water. Adding cyclohexane separates them: one layer goes purple, the other stays yellow-orange. Identify each.
check.modelAnswer: The purple layer marks iodide, oxidised to iodine that collects purple in the organic phase; the yellow-orange layer marks bromide, whose bromine product keeps its yellow-orange shade in the organic layer.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which a more reactive halogen pushes a less reactive halogen out of its halide solution.
An ion present in the mixture whose oxidation number is unchanged, so it is omitted from the ionic equation.
A balanced equation showing only the species that actually change oxidation state during the reaction.
